subsection: 2. Irish trading patterns with the EU

points: Before 1973 Irish trade depended on the UK. In 1960 about three-quarters (74%) of Irish exports went to the UK, mainly live cattle and other farm produce.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement, signed in 1965, governed trade with the UK. Protectionism was dismantled from the late 1950s.
Ireland joined the EEC on 1 January 1973, together with the UK and Denmark, after a referendum on 10 May 1972 returned about 83% Yes.
The UK's share of Irish exports fell from about three-quarters in 1960 to a small fraction today. In February 2024 Great Britain took about 8% of Irish goods exports in that month alone.
As the UK's share fell, the rest of the EU and the USA became far more important.

Exports moved from mainly agricultural goods and live animals to high-value manufactured goods. Pharmaceuticals and chemicals, medical devices, and computers and electronics grew strongly in the 1990s and 2000s.
Processed food and drink replaced live animals as the main farm exports, and services became a larger part of the economy's trade.
Exports far exceed imports. Ireland has a very large goods trade surplus, mainly because foreign multinationals export most of what they make in Ireland.
Goods exports were about €224 billion in 2024, a record and up about 14% on 2023.
Goods imports were about €135 billion, giving a goods surplus of about €89 billion.
The EU 27 took about €88 billion of Irish goods exports in 2024, about 40%, making it the largest bloc.
The USA took about €73 billion, about one-third of exports, and is Ireland's largest single export market.
The main EU markets in 2024 were the Netherlands (about €23 billion), Germany (about €20 billion), Belgium (about €17 billion) and then France.
The EU 27 supplied about €50 billion of Irish imports in 2024, about 37%, making it the largest bloc.
Asia supplied about €31 billion, the USA about €23 billion and the UK about €22 billion. Asia, especially China, is growing as a source of imports.
Medical and pharmaceutical products are the largest export group, at about €100 billion in 2024 (about 45% of goods exports).
Organic chemicals, medical devices, and food and drink follow as the other main exports.
Fuels, because Ireland imports most of its energy.
Machinery and transport equipment, including aircraft for the leasing industry.
Chemicals, consumer goods and food.
Preliminary CSO figures show goods exports of about €260 billion in 2025, up about 16% and a record. Pharmaceutical exports to the USA were brought forward before threatened US tariffs.
Medical and pharmaceutical products were about €139 billion in 2025, about 53% of goods exports.
The USA took about 43% of exports in 2025. Imports were about €144 billion.
Exports to the USA fell sharply at the end of 2025. The EU-USA deal of July 2025 capped US tariffs on most EU goods, including pharmaceuticals, at 15%.
The surge shows how dependent the totals are on one product and one market. 2024 is the better guide to a typical year.
Ireland is a major exporter of services, especially computer and software services sold by multinationals such as Google, Meta and Microsoft, whose European headquarters are in Dublin.
Financial services are based at the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in Dublin Docklands, which opened in 1987. Aircraft leasing is another major service.
Much of this services trade is sold into EU markets from an Irish base.
Ireland exports about 90% of its beef and dairy output, and produces far more food than its population eats.
Food, drink and horticulture exports were about €17 billion in 2024, a record and up about 5% (Bord Bia).
Of these exports, about 35% (about €5.9 billion) went to the EU and about €5.2 billion to markets outside the EU and UK; the UK took the remainder, about a third.
Dairy, at about €6.3 billion, was the largest category.
The UK remains the largest single market for Irish food.
Meat and livestock exports in 2024 went about 44% to the EU and about 42% to the UK.
Kerrygold butter, marketed by Ornua (formerly the Irish Dairy Board), sells in Germany, one of its biggest markets, and other EU countries.
Irish beef is sold through EU retailers, and Irish whiskey and Baileys are sold internationally.

notes.h: Why Ireland trades so heavily with the EU
points: Single market access: tariff-free and barrier-free trade with about 450 million consumers in 2024.
The euro: Ireland adopted it in 1999 and notes and coins followed in 2002. Trade with eurozone countries carries no exchange-rate risk.
Sterling fell sharply after the UK referendum of 23 June 2016, which hurt Irish food exporters to the UK.
CAP access and common standards opened EU food markets to Irish farm produce. The CAP is covered in How the EU influences the Irish economy.
US and other multinationals locate in Ireland to supply the EU market from inside it. Examples include Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare (since 1989), Apple in Cork (since 1980) and Pfizer.
Ireland attracts them with an English-speaking, educated workforce, a corporation tax rate of 12.5%, and support from IDA Ireland, the state agency that attracts foreign investment.
From 2024 firms with turnover over €750 million pay a minimum tax of 15%. The multinationals themselves are covered in The Global Economy notes.
Ireland is an island on the periphery of Europe, so most trade goes by sea.
Dublin Port is Ireland's largest port. Rosslare Europort in Co. Wexford is the main port for direct ferries to continental Europe. Cork and Shannon Foynes also handle trade.
High-value, light goods such as pharmaceuticals and electronics go by air.
The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020. The transition ended on 31 December 2020, and the Trade and Cooperation Agreement has applied since 1 January 2021.
Trade with Great Britain now crosses an EU external border, with customs declarations and checks on food and animals.

The UK landbridge, trucks crossing Britain to reach the continent, became slower. From 2 January 2021 DFDS ran a direct Rosslare-Dunkirk freight ferry, six times a week. By April 2021 there were about 36 direct weekly sailings from Rosslare to continental Europe.
Rosslare also has direct sailings to Cherbourg, Saint-Malo and Roscoff in France, and to Bilbao in Spain.

Imports from Great Britain fell after 2021 as some importers switched to EU suppliers. Cross-border trade with Northern Ireland grew, because Northern Ireland stays in the EU single market for goods under the Windsor Framework of February 2023, covered in The complexity of regions (i).
Brexit raised the share of Irish trade with the rest of the EU and reduced Ireland's dependence on the UK further.
Over-reliance on a few multinationals, one sector (pharmaceuticals) and one market (the USA) leaves exports exposed to US tariffs and to corporate decisions.
Ireland's peripheral location adds transport costs, so sea links to the continent are vital.

keyTerms.definition: The 1965 agreement that governed Irish trade with the UK before Ireland joined the EEC.
The route by road across Great Britain used to carry goods between Ireland and continental Europe, made slower after Brexit.
A sailing that carries goods from Ireland straight to continental Europe without crossing Great Britain, such as Rosslare to Dunkirk.
Investment by a company based in another country to set up or buy operations in a host country.
A company that operates production or service facilities in more than one country.
The tax a company pays on its profits; Ireland's rate is 12.5%, with a 15% minimum for the largest firms from 2024.
The amount by which the value of goods exports is greater than the value of goods imports.
Bringing forward exports or purchases before an expected tariff or price change, which inflates the figures for that period.
The February 2023 arrangement that keeps Northern Ireland in the EU single market for goods.
Exports of food, drink and horticultural products, mainly beef and dairy for Ireland.

factCards.term: Irish trade before 1973: main market, main exports and the key agreement
factCards.definition: In 1960 about three-quarters (74%) of Irish exports went to the UK, mainly live cattle and other farm produce. Trade with the UK was governed by the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965); protectionism was dismantled from the late 1950s.

factCards.definition: Ireland joined on 1 January 1973, together with the UK and Denmark, after a referendum on 10 May 1972 returned about 83% Yes.

factCards.term: Irish export markets since 1973: how they diversified
factCards.definition: The UK's share fell from about three-quarters in 1960 to a small fraction today (Great Britain took under a tenth of goods exports in February 2024), while the rest of the EU and the USA became far more important.

factCards.term: Irish exports since 1973: how the products changed
factCards.definition: From mainly farm goods and live animals to high-value manufactures: pharmaceuticals and chemicals, medical devices, and computers and electronics, which grew strongly in the 1990s and 2000s. Processed food and drink replaced live animals, and services grew.

factCards.definition: Goods exports about €224 billion, a record, up about 14% on 2023; imports about €135 billion; a surplus of about €89 billion (CSO). The surplus is large mainly because foreign multinationals export most of what they make in Ireland.

The EU 27 is the largest bloc, about €88 billion (about 40%); the USA is the largest single country, about €73 billion (about one-third). Main EU markets: the Netherlands about €23 billion, Germany about €20 billion, Belgium about €17 billion, then France.

factCards.term: Ireland's main sources of goods imports (2024)
factCards.definition: The EU 27 is the largest bloc, about €50 billion (about 37%); then Asia about €31 billion, the USA about €23 billion and the UK about €22 billion. Asia, especially China, is a growing source.
Medical and pharmaceutical products are the largest group, about €100 billion (about 45% of goods exports); then organic chemicals, medical devices, and food and drink.

factCards.term: Ireland's main goods imports, and why fuels are one
factCards.definition: Fuels, because Ireland imports most of its energy; machinery and transport equipment, including aircraft for the leasing industry; chemicals; consumer goods; food.

factCards.term: The 2025 Irish export surge: what happened and the risk it shows
factCards.definition: Pharmaceuticals were rushed to the USA before threatened tariffs: goods exports about €260 billion (up about 16%), pharma about €139 billion (53%), the USA about 43% (CSO, preliminary). It shows reliance on a few firms, one sector and one market.

factCards.term: Ireland's services exports: the three main types
factCards.definition: Software and computer services from multinationals such as Google, Meta and Microsoft, with European headquarters in Dublin; financial services at the IFSC, Dublin Docklands (opened 1987); aircraft leasing. Much is sold into EU markets.

factCards.term: Irish agri-food exports (2024): value, markets and largest category
factCards.definition: About 90% of beef and dairy output is exported. Food, drink and horticulture exports were a record €17 billion (Bord Bia): about 35% (€5.9 billion) to the EU, €5.2 billion to international markets, about a third to the UK. Dairy (€6.3 billion) leads.

factCards.term: Irish food exports: the UK's role, meat markets and named brands
factCards.definition: The UK is still the largest single market for Irish food; meat and livestock went about 44% to the EU and 42% to the UK (2024). Brands: Kerrygold butter (marketed by Ornua, formerly the Irish Dairy Board) in Germany and other EU markets, and Baileys.

factCards.term: Why Ireland trades heavily with the EU: single market, euro and CAP
factCards.definition: Tariff-free access to about 450 million consumers (2024); the euro (adopted 1999, notes 2002) removes exchange-rate risk, while sterling's fall after the June 2016 referendum hurt food exporters to the UK; CAP and common standards open EU food markets.

factCards.term: Foreign direct investment as a reason for Irish trade with the EU
factCards.definition: Multinationals locate in Ireland to supply the EU from inside: Intel at Leixlip (since 1989), Apple in Cork (since 1980), Pfizer. They come for an English-speaking, educated workforce, 12.5% corporation tax (15% for the largest from 2024) and IDA Ireland.

factCards.term: How Irish goods reach the EU: ports, air freight and the periphery
factCards.definition: As an island on the periphery, Ireland sends most trade by sea: Dublin Port (the largest), Rosslare Europort (direct ferries to the continent), Cork and Shannon Foynes. Light, high-value pharmaceuticals and electronics go by air; distance adds costs.

factCards.term: Brexit: dates, and the new costs for Irish trade with Great Britain
factCards.definition: The UK left on 31 January 2020; transition ended 31 December 2020; the Trade and Cooperation Agreement applied from 1 January 2021. Trade with Great Britain now crosses an EU external border, with customs declarations and checks on food and animals.

factCards.term: Brexit: the growth of direct ferries from Rosslare
factCards.definition: DFDS began a direct Rosslare–Dunkirk freight ferry on 2 January 2021, six times a week, to avoid the UK landbridge; by April 2021 there were about 36 direct weekly sailings to the continent. Rosslare also sails direct to Cherbourg, Saint-Malo, Roscoff and Bilbao.

factCards.term: Brexit: three effects on the pattern of Irish trade
factCards.definition: Imports from Great Britain fell as some importers switched to EU suppliers; cross-border trade with Northern Ireland grew, as the Windsor Framework (February 2023) keeps it in the single market for goods; the rest of the EU's share of Irish trade rose.

questions.prompt: Examine how Ireland's trading patterns with the European Union have changed since Ireland joined in 1973.
questions.model: Before 1973 Ireland depended on the UK: in 1960 about three-quarters of Irish exports went there, mainly live cattle and farm produce, under the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement of 1965. Since joining the EEC on 1 January 1973, Ireland has diversified. The UK's share fell from about three-quarters to a small fraction, while the rest of the EU and the USA grew. The product mix changed from live animals and farm goods to high-value manufactured goods. In 2024 goods exports were about €224 billion and imports about €135 billion, a surplus of about €89 billion. The EU 27 took about 40% of exports (about €88 billion) and the USA about one-third (about €73 billion), the largest single market. Pharmaceuticals are the largest export group, about €100 billion or about 45%. Factors behind the pattern include the single market, which gives tariff-free access to about 450 million consumers; foreign direct investment by multinationals such as Intel and Apple, which supply the EU from Ireland; the euro, which removes exchange-rate risk within the eurozone; and the Common Agricultural Policy, which opened EU food markets to Irish beef and dairy. Food, drink and horticulture exports were about €17 billion in 2024, with about 35% going to the EU. Brexit has added customs checks on trade with Great Britain and shifted trade further towards the EU, with direct ferries from Rosslare to continental Europe from 2021. Over-reliance on pharmaceuticals and the USA is a risk, as the 2025 surge showed.

questions.prompt: Explain how Brexit has affected Ireland's trade with the EU and the UK.
questions.model: The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, so trade with Great Britain now crosses an external border with customs declarations and checks on food and animals. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement has applied since 1 January 2021. The UK landbridge became slower and more costly, so from 2 January 2021 DFDS ran direct Rosslare to Dunkirk freight sailings, and by April 2021 there were about 36 direct weekly sailings from Rosslare to continental Europe. Food exporters depend on the UK, which remains the largest single market for Irish food, and sterling's fall after the 2016 referendum added currency risk to UK trade. Imports from Great Britain fell after 2021 as some importers switched to EU suppliers. Cross-border trade with Northern Ireland grew under the Windsor Framework. Brexit has increased the share of Irish trade with the rest of the EU and reduced dependence on the UK.

questions.prompt: Explain one advantage of EU membership for Irish trade.
questions.model: Membership gives Irish exporters tariff-free access to the single market of about 450 million consumers. Irish beef and dairy, of which about 90% is exported, benefit from the common market and the common standards that open EU food markets to them.
